title: Steer a laser onto a detector with two mirrors, blocking the beam while they move
instruction: The laser is always on: its beam runs 4 cm above the table between the two red lines. Use the two silver mirrors to steer the beam onto the centre of the yellow detector's front face, reflecting it off both mirrors. Never move a mirror while the beam is on it: put the orange beam block in the beam first and take it out once both mirrors are set. Never let the beam leave the table, and let go of everything at the end.
context: Photonics technicians (O*NET 17-3029.08) build and align the laser and optical test benches behind fibre-optic and photonics manufacturing, including the optical interconnects of AI hardware, steering beams with mirrors every day. Laser-safety practice (ANSI Z136.1 and the lab procedures built on it) says to block the beam before inserting or moving an optic and to keep every beam terminated on the table, because a mirror swung through a live beam throws a stray reflection across the room at eye height. Here the laser stays on and its beam is not drawn: the robot must work out the mirror angles from the layout, place them precisely, and keep the beam safe while it changes the scene. The beam is in reach of the left arm only and the right mirror starts in reach of the right arm only, so both arms are needed for a path off both mirrors. The safety rules are scored at every control step, not only at the end.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm; the table runs from x -19 to 91 cm and from y -65 to +65 cm. Everything below is fixed to the table unless called loose. (1) Laser: the blue aluminium housing of an always-on, low-power alignment laser, 40 x 40 mm and 60 mm tall, centred at x 12.0 cm, y +24.0 cm; its beam leaves the middle of its front (+x) face, 40 mm above the table, and runs along +x. The beam is not drawn in the simulation. (2) Beam dump: a black anodized aluminium box 30 mm along x, 60 mm along y, 60 mm tall, centred at x 50.0 cm, y +24.0 cm, where the beam ends at the start. (3) Two thin red plastic strips (lines) glued on the table, 10 mm wide and 2 mm tall, from x 14.5 to 48.0 cm, centred at y +18.5 and +29.5 cm: the beam runs midway between them. (4) Detector: a yellow plastic sensor head 20 mm along x, 40 mm along y, 60 mm tall, centred at x 20.0 cm, y -16.0 cm; its sensitive face is its front (+x) face, at x 21.0 cm, and its centre is the point on that face midway across and 40 mm above the table (beam height). (5) Backstop: a black painted plywood board 10 mm along x, 200 mm along y, 60 mm tall, centred at x 17.0 cm, y -16.0 cm, behind the detector. (6) Two thin black plastic strips (lines) glued on the table, 10 mm wide and 2 mm tall, from x 21.5 to 40.0 cm, centred at y -10.5 and -21.5 cm, either side of the detector's axis. (7) Two mirrors, loose: each a double-sided flat mirror, one silver box 20 mm thick, 60 mm wide and 60 mm tall, 80 g: a plastic mount with a 40 x 40 x 2 mm glass mirror set in the middle of each 60 x 60 mm face, framed by a 10 mm rim. Only the two 40 x 40 mm mirrors reflect; the rims and the 20 mm edges do not (the simulation draws the whole box silver). The left mirror stands centred at x 32.0 cm, y +38.0 cm, the right mirror at x 24.0 cm, y -36.0 cm, each with its faces toward +x and -x (its 60 mm width along y). (8) Beam block: a loose orange box of painted softwood, 40 x 40 mm and 60 mm tall, 60 g, standing centred at x 20.0 cm, y +36.0 cm, sides parallel to x and y. Nothing else is on the table. The right arm cannot reach the beam's starting path and the left arm cannot reach the right mirror's starting place.
scoring: The laser is always on. Every control step the scorer traces the beam in 3-D from the laser's aperture (x 14.0 cm, y +24.0 cm, 40 mm up, along +x) through every object's box, at its current position and orientation: it reflects off a mirror's 40 x 40 mm glass on either face (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; a tilted mirror sends it up or down) and stops on anything else it meets: the block, the dump, the backstop, the laser, the detector, a mirror's 10 mm rim or 20 mm edge, or the table top. The arms neither stop nor reflect it. The beam is 'stray' if it leaves the table's outline without being stopped. A mirror is 'lit' while the beam meets it anywhere (glass, rim or edge). Rules: (1) the beam is stray; (2) a lit mirror moves more than 3 mm or turns more than 1 degree from where it stood at the last control step before the beam came onto it, checked at every lit step and at the first step after the beam leaves it, so swinging a mirror into or out of the beam between two steps counts (a mirror kept dark behind the block may be moved freely); (3) a mirror or the block falls off the table (its lowest point more than 10 mm below the table top). A gripper has 'let go' when its opening is 0.9 or more (fingers at least 84.5 mm apart) or its fingers are more than 10 mm from both mirrors and the block; the scorer reads each gripper's tool point, finger-tip point and opening from the embodiment's state, and, not knowing which way it is turned, counts its fingers as a round zone about its axis out to their outer corners, from the tips to 38 mm up. Score 0 if any rule is broken at any moment, whatever happens afterwards. Otherwise, from the beam at the end: 1.0 if it reflects off both mirrors and stops on the detector's front face within 10 mm of its centre, with both grippers let go; 0.75 if it reflects off both mirrors and stops on the detector's front face, but further than 10 mm from its centre or with a gripper not let go; 0.5 if it reflects off both mirrors and stops anywhere else on the table (the backstop, the dump, the table top, ...); 0.25 if it reflects off one mirror only and stops on the table; 0 if it reflects off no mirror (the block still in the beam, or no mirror in it). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. The score is read at the last step: the trial ends early once the 1.0 conditions have held with both mirrors and the block still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. On a step where the grippers' state cannot be read, 'both grippers let go' is taken as met (the trace counts such steps). A simulator state with a non-finite number scores 0 for that step. In a real trial the laser is a visible low-power one: cards along the table edges and video from above show rules 1 and 2, and the detector's output or a target card on its face gives the spot.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, default friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Laser, dump, detector, backstop and lines are fixed; the mirrors and block are uniform boxes (mirrors all silver, rims not drawn). The beam is not simulated or drawn: the scorer traces an ideal ray through the objects' true boxes, mirror glass a perfect reflector, every other surface a stop. The arms are left out of the beam model. The scorer reads each gripper's tool and tip points and opening, not its heading.
reset_notes: Stand both mirrors and the block back on their starting places, upright, sides parallel to x and y (mirror faces toward +x and -x). The laser, dump, detector, backstop and lines are fixed. Nothing is consumed. On a real bench, switch the laser off or close its shutter while resetting.
